https://globalvoices.org/2026/08/07/what.text: What does home mean for people with no single territory connecting them? An image from a documentary about a Roma soldier reintegrating into civilian life after joining the Ukrainian Armed Forces. Hundreds of Roma soldiers enlisted to defend Ukraine after Russia’s second full-scale invasion began in February 2022. Screenshot from YouTube . This post is part of Global Voices’ July 2026 Spotlight series, “ Statelessness .” This series offers insight into the issue of statelessness and how it hinders people’s freedom of movement, educational opportunities, political access, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here . While trying to define nationhood, people often rely on simplistic descriptions and groupings — the lines drawn on a map, demarcations outlined by treaties and agreements, common identities and ideologies within a specific space — but for many people groups, the concept of nationhood can fall outside these traditional borders. This is the case for many in post-Soviet spaces, for example, Ukraine’s Roma community, whose members are now fighting Russia and dying for a country that, for generations, treated them as outsiders. It is also true for Tatars, whose homeland largely exists within a cultural space rather than a physical one. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022 , hundreds of Roma have joined the Armed Forces of Ukraine in the fight against Russia. Yet despite this service, Roma Ukrainian refugees continue facing discrimination within Ukraine and beyond in Europe. Further east, within Russia, Tatars , the country’s second-largest ethnic group, continue to grapple with a different question: What does homeland mean for a people scattered across continents, with no single territory uniting them? Tatarstan , a republic of the Russian Federation, remains a cultural anchor, but for many Tatars, belonging is carried through community and culture rather than a location on a map. That dispersion, together with a traumatic, fraught history, shapes how Tatars today navigate conversations about sovereignty, separatism, and self-determination. In this collaborative article, Global Voices contributors explore these two stories of statelessness and reveal how minority communities are redefining nationhood, loyalty, and identity across the region. The Ukrainian Roma fighting Russia, yet still not accepted Since the second Russian large-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, there have been few stories of Ukraine’s Roma population fighting for Ukraine, even as many took to the front lines. A photo of Roma soldiers in the Ukrainian Armed Forces holding a Roma flag alongside Ukrainian flags. Photo via Myroslav Horvat’s Facebook . Fair use. Already in 2022, Roma journalist Viktor Chovka reported that Roma soldiers were fighting within the Ukrainian Army because they were born in Ukraine and considered it their home . Myroslav Horvat, another Romani activist in Ukraine, told Swedish Radio Romano at that time that most Romani people were concerned about how they would make a living because they lost their jobs when the war began. On his Facebook profile , Horvat often shares photographs of Romani soldiers in the Ukrainian Army. His main photo also features the Ukrainian flag, highlighting the dual identities that many Ukrainian Roma carry. According to Horvat, approximately 250 Roma from Zakarpattia joined Ukraine’s defense forces in 2022. By August 2024, he estimated that more than 500 were serving. Ukrainian flags have become increasingly visible in Roma settlements , alongside greater use of the Ukrainian language and Ukrainian songs. In an article from 2024 by the Ukrainian media outlet Varosh , Horvat said Roma people historically lived as minorities under various states and empires and rarely occupied secure social positions. Their experience of persecution during the Second World War also contributed to a historical distance from military institutions. Today, however, many equate defending Ukraine to defending their own families and future. Horvat also mentions educational inequality: He estimates that around 40 percent of Roma in Zakarpattia, Ukraine, lack a basic secondary education , although the situation has improved in recent years. Some Roma have never obtained Ukrainian passports , which can prevent them from being formally mobilized. Regional recruitment officials say low literacy does not necessarily prevent military service, but it can create practical difficulties. Anti-Discrimination Center “Memorial” organized a meeting in 2025 in Brussels with Roma veterans who voluntarily joined the Armed Forces of Ukraine , where Roma veterans described both discrimination and solidarity within the Ukrainian armed forces. Roma Arsen Mednyk joined the military after Russian forces occupied his hometown, Bucha , and massacred civilians there. Initially treated with suspicion because he was Roma, he earned the trust of other soldiers and later became a storm-unit commander. His story was presented in a documentary about Roma soldiers and the war . Marginalization and discrimination of Roma refugees Romani people living in Lviv. License CC BY-SA 2.5 via Wikimedia Commons . Before February 2022, Ukraine’s Roma population already faced severe barriers to citizenship, housing, education, healthcare, and employment. Of an estimated 400,000 Roma living in the country, around 30,000 reportedly lacked official identity documents, leaving them functionally stateless . Roma women sometimes gave birth at home because of discrimination or unaffordable medical costs, leaving children without birth certificates and forcing families to live at the margins of society. Roma communities were also sometimes targeted by nationalist groups and were often the victims of discrimination and prejudice. After the Russian invasion, discrimination followed Roma families to Ukraine’s borders. Human rights organizations received reports of unequal treatment, including a case of a mother and two children who were repeatedly prevented from crossing into Hungary. In European reception centers, Roma refugees were sometimes segregated from other Ukrainians. In Moldova, families were placed in facilities without adequate heating or hot water. In the Czech Republic , the Guardian reported in 2022, Roma slept in poor conditions at Prague’s railway station and were accused of pretending to be Ukrainian to obtain assistance. Volunteers also reported that some hosts in Moldova and Poland were willing to accommodate only white refugees , while the Roma are widely considered people of color . For some families, the hostility was so intense that they chose to return to war-torn Ukraine rather than remain in discriminatory conditions. For Tatars, homeland is more than a place on the map While the war has pushed many Ukrainian Roma to defend a land they consider theirs, f or Tatars, however, the relationship between identity and territory has never been so simple. The Tatarstan flag. License CC BY-SA 3.0 RS via Wikimedia Commons . Tatars are the second-largest ethnic nation in the Russian Federation, yet there is no single place that all Tatars call home. The Republic of Tatarstan , a territory within Russia, is often described as the homeland of the Tatars , but ethnic Tatars make up only around half of the republic’s population, sharing it with Russians, Bashkirs, Chuvash, Armenians and many others. Beyond Tatarstan, millions of Tatars live across Russia, in neighboring republics, oblasts, krais and major cities, as well as throughout the post-Soviet space and in diasporas across Europe, Türkiye, North America and beyond. Some communities were formed through centuries of imperial expansion , forced resettlement and Soviet policies, while others emerged through education, work or personal choice. As a result, Tatar identity has long existed across borders rather than within them. Crimean Tartar women in traditional dresses. Tartars have long had their own distinct culture, traditions, music, and dress. Image from Wikimedia Commons . License CC BY-SA 4.0 . This dispersion has shaped how many Tatars understand belonging. Tatarstan remains the historical and cultural center of the nation, home to institutions that preserve the language , literature, and traditions. But for many Tatars, “homeland” is just as likely to be found around a family table , through the Tatar language , music, Sabantuy celebrations or even the ritual of sharing tea as it is on a map. The culture has become the thread connecting communities separated by geography, politics and generations. For a people spread across continents, identity is often carried rather than inherited from a single place. A Tatar Woman at the May 18 commemoration of the Crimean Tatar deportations and genocide at Maidan Square, Kyiv, Ukraine. Image from Wikimedia Commons . License CC BY-SA 2.0 . This also explains why conversations about the future of Tatarstan often sound different inside Tatar communities than they do abroad. Previous attempts to link Tatar national aspirations to geopolitical projects, including the German -sponsored Idel-Ural Legion during World War II and the collaboration of some Crimean Tatar groups with Nazi occupation authorities, were followed by devastating consequences, most notably the collective deportation of the Crimean Tatars in 1944. These episodes continue to influence how many Tatars perceive questions of sovereignty and separatism. Some commentators, including contributors regularly featured by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), the Idel-Ural project, and affiliated platforms , have argued that Russia’s republics should become independent states if the Russian Federation were ever to disintegrate. Yet such discussions do not necessarily reflect the views of many Tatars themselves. With Tatars living across the Russian Federation and far beyond its borders, and with Tatarstan located in the geographical heart of European Russia rather than on its periphery, the republic holds a significance that is primarily historical, cultural, and symbolic. For many Tatars, as for other minorities in Russia, preserving language, culture and community remains a more immediate concern than redrawing political borders. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.text: Image source, EPA By Florence Freeman Published 3 September 2026 Around 2,000 students and teachers across Indonesia have fallen ill with food poisoning over the past three days linked to the government's free school meals programme. In the latest case, 777 people became unwell after consuming the food at a high school in Rembang, Central Java, the institution's headteacher said. The meals were provided through a multibillion-dollar scheme that is one of President Prabowo Subianto's signature policies, aiming to improve nutrition for Indonesia's schoolchildren. But, as well as being the suspected source of a string of mass food poisonings, the programme has been dogged by allegations of corruption and criticism of its cost. A total of 752 students and 25 teachers experienced symptoms of food poisoning after eating meals provided through the Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG) programme at the high school in Lasem on Wednesday lunchtime. "They had diarrhoea and took turns using the toilet," headteacher Juhartutik told BBC News Indonesia. "There are 40 toilets in total, so they can't accommodate everyone." The school has since sent nearly 1,200 pupils and 95 members of staff home, while several were taken to hospital. Juhartutik said the government would cover any medical costs and that the local food distributor had come to the school to "take responsibility". The suspected outbreak came after 730 people fell ill after consuming MBG meals at an Islamic boarding school in Sidoarjo, East Java, on Tuesday, a local health official said. Reni said their child felt dizzy and nauseous before developing stomach problems after eating the meal. Some of those affected required hospital treatment, with some students being transported in wheelchairs because they were too weak to stand. Hundreds of others have been affected by suspected cases of food poisoning linked to the free school meals this week, including hundreds across several schools in Tana Toraja, South Sulawesi. Improper storage or poorly prepared food are often to blame for cases of food poisoning, in which the body rejects the contaminated food. Parents and teachers have told reporters of slimy chicken, as well as food that appeared undercooked and had a fishy odour. Local authorities are investigating the cause of the suspected outbreaks, with food samples being tested for possible contamination. The head of the food distribution unit in Lasem, Achmad Sholeh Syarifudin, apologised and took "full responsibility for the recovery of students and teachers". He said the unit would conduct a comprehensive evaluation of its operation following the incident. The head of Indonesia's National Nutrition Agency has said: "If it is identified that there was negligence and there are criminal elements, I apologise, we cannot help." https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-blast.text: DUBLIN — Serbia’s public commemorations for convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić risk undermining the country’s relationship with the EU, the bloc has warned ahead of the funeral of the man dubbed the “Butcher of Bosnia.” The former commander of the Bosnian Serb Army during the 1992-1995 Bosnian War died behind bars in The Hague last week, where he was serving a life sentence for crimes against humanity. His coffin was draped in a Serbian flag and flown to Belgrade in a government plane on Thursday, and is due to be buried after a service at the House of the Army on Monday, with thousands expected to attend. The EU’s enlargement commissioner, Marta Kos, told POLITICO that public support for Mladić was incompatible with Serbia’s application to join the EU. Advertisement Advertisement “The glorification of war criminals has no place; it goes really, really strong against European values and has no space, not in the EU member states, but also in our candidates,” she said. “We are observing the situation very carefully … and we will see what will happen in [the] next days and we also see the actions of the government,” Kos added. “There is for sure a place for Serbia in the EU, but [the EU] demands not just doing the reforms. The strategic alliances or strategic orientation on the field of common security and foreign policy is getting even more and more important.” A Serbian government official, granted anonymity to speak frankly, insisted the state was not directly involved in Monday’s proceedings. “⁠The commemorative gathering is being organized not by the Ministry of Defense or the General Staff of the Serbian Armed Forces, but by the Association of Retired Generals,” they said, adding that Mladić will not receive the honor of being buried in either the Alley of the Greats or the Alley of Distinguished Citizens. Under Mladić’s command, the Bosnian Serb Army laid siege to Sarajevo for almost four years, cutting off supplies to the civilian population and turning its streets into sniper lanes in which thousands of civilians were shot. Mladić was found to be responsible by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia for the massacre of more than 8,000 Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica, as well as atrocities committed by his troops across the country. The 2011 capture of Mladić, who had been in hiding for almost a decade, came months before Serbia was awarded EU candidate status, paving the way for significant financial and administrative support from the bloc. The decision to extradite him to face justice in The Hague was controversial in Serbia, with polling at the time showing as many as 40 percent of Serbs viewed him as a hero . Tributes were held in majority-Serb towns and cities across Bosnia following his death. Prominent Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik said “Mladić was respected by the Serbian people. As a commander he stood to defend Serbs.” Advertisement Advertisement Ireland’s Europe Minister Thomas Byrne, who is chairing a meeting of EU candidate countries in Dublin on Friday, said that while “there’s not actually a state funeral taking place … there may well be senior figures from government memorializing that man, so that’s not acceptable.” “It is certainly time to bury the past and to work and continue reconciliation in that region,” Byrne added. “What’s happening there, I think, continues to hurt people, particularly in the region, but also in some member states of the European Union in particular.” Mladić will be buried at Topčider Cemetery in Belgrade on Monday.

https://aa.com.tr/en/europe/at-least-2-p.text: Europe At least 2 people injured in explosion at German train station, police report Train station currently closed, with train services disrupted and rerouted to other tracks Oliver Towfigh Nia 02 September 2026 • Update : 02 September 2026 BERLIN At least two people sustained minor injuries in an explosion at a train station in the southern German city of Augsburg, police reported Wednesday. The station building and Track 1 are currently closed, a police spokesperson told daily Bild Wednesday morning. Train service is disrupted and is being rerouted to the other tracks. Window panes were also damaged by the explosion. Explosives experts from the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office are on the scene, according to police. The cause of the explosion is still unknown. Public transportation around the train station building has also been affected. Police are also investigating suspected sabotage at an Amprion power substation in Bergheim, in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, public broadcaster WDR reported. A short circuit knocked several power lines out of operation, but the wider electricity supply was unaffected. Police suspect the incident was deliberate rather than the result of a technical fault. Investigators are examining whether it could be connected to the suspected sabotage in Brandenburg. Suspected sabotage at Brandenburg power plant The incident came after unidentified suspects carried out a sabotage attack on an electrical facility at a major power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday, according to authorities. Brandenburg Interior Minister Jan Redmann said the suspects used projectile devices to cause a short circuit in an extra-high-voltage line near the Jaenschwalde power plant. “We cannot currently confirm that an explosive device detonated there or anything of that sort,” Redmann said. Police earlier said devices apparently made from pyrotechnics had been found at an electrical substation, although reports differed over whether any of them exploded. Bild reported that police had confirmed an explosion and discovered several improvised incendiary and explosive devices, not all of which detonated. Public broadcaster RBB, however, quoted police spokesperson Stefanie Pilz as saying that no explosion had occurred. Grid operator 50Hertz said unknown perpetrators damaged several transmission lines, briefly interrupting operations. All lines were later restored, and the public electricity supply was unaffected. The Jaenschwalde facility near the Polish border is one of Germany’s largest lignite-fired power stations. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription LATEST NEWS All IMO urges member states to stop attacking merchant ships Global markets trade mixed ahead of Fed’s rate decision Yemeni army targets Houthi positions in western Taiz Kosovo's ex-President Thaci sentenced to 25 years for war crimes EU to introduce common age limit for social media EU Commission chief calls for new European Security Council,' bloc-wide emergency security protocol Türkiye, Azerbaijan are '2 islands of stability' in region: Turkish foreign minister See All Luxembourg ends role approving Israeli bond prospectus for European markets German police report sabotage attack on power grid near Cologne

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text: Sustainable ways of living: interior of the the Aalto House, Helsinki Photograph: 2026 Tuomas Uusheimo: www.uush View image in fullscreen Sustainable ways of living: interior of the the Aalto House, Helsinki Photograph: 2026 Tuomas Uusheimo: www.uush Architecture Home is where the jellyfish glows: Finland finally warms to nature-loving modernist Alvar Aalto His egalitarian homeland used to harbour reservation against the architecture star. But with 13 new Unesco listings and a new exhibition in Helsinki, Aalto’s work is finally getting the recognition it deserves Christian House Tue 13 Oct 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I n the early 1950s, Alvar Aalto built a boat to get to his remote summer residence on an island in Lake Päijänne, about 200km north of Helsinki . But the celebrated Finnish architect was not a happy skipper. He named the boat – a title as cumbersome as his buildings were elegant – Nemo propheta in patria: “No man is a prophet in his own land”. The name was a dig at Finland , which the architectural maestro believed had taken him for granted. Other nations, he moaned, recognised his talent more than his own. Today, arriving in Helsinki, I find that Finland doesn’t just love Aalto, he’s a national treasure. Last month, 13 Alvar sites dotted around Finland gained Unesco world heritage status. In addition to this international honour, vast quantities of Finnish public funding are being spent on the restoration of his buildings, and his designs are currently being celebrated in the Aalto Design – Shapes of Wellbeing exhibition at Helsinki’s Architecture & Design Museum. Norman Foster could but dream of such public adoration. For many Finns today, Aalto’s buildings – light-filled, harmonious habitats created from the mid-1920s to his death in 1976 – speak of national pride at a time of geopolitical tension with Russia and, further afield, connect to global considerations about “wellness” in the built environment. View image in fullscreen Glacier-like: Finlandia Hall, Helsinki Photograph: © 2026 Kuvatoimisto Kuvio Oy and Helsinki Partners But was it true that Aalto was once underappreciated at home? “The boat’s name wasn’t entirely in jest,” notes Sofia Nivarti, author of Studio Aalto, a new survey of his work to be published later this month. “The more he succeeded internationally, the more a local audience turned against him – steeped in a social-democratic ethos of egalitarianism, Finnish architectural circles worried about the dominance of one name over all others.” In the first half of the 1950s, Aalto “wasn’t able to get a professorship from his alma mater, the Helsinki University of Technology,” explains Tommi Lindh, CEO of the Alvar Aalto Foundation. And a starchitect’s ego is a fragile thing, even in the cool egalitarian north. In Helsinki, Lindh gives me a tour of the National Pensions Institute – now home to the Finns’ social security system – a vast brick building designed by Aalto between 1953 and 1957. It is perfectly preserved, right down to its ingenious overhead heating panels, angled skylights and working paternoster lift. This monumental brick building is one of five Aalto sites in Helsinki to gain Unesco recognition, alongside the House of Culture (commissioned by the Finnish Communist party in 1952, with the goal of “making culture the property of the entire nation”), Finlandia Hall, the vast, glacier-like concert and conference centre, and both Aalto’s home and his studio. View image in fullscreen As if it’s been bent by the wind … a chair by Aalto. Photograph: Foundation for the Finnish Museum of Architecture and Design At the Shapes of Wellbeing exhibition, curators have broadened out the Aalto story to include the work of Alvar’s first wife, Aino, and second wife, Elissa, both skilled architects in their own right. It also shows that the experiential – and nature-loving – considerations Aalto brought to buildings also shaped his approach to furniture and lighting systems: his pendant lights recall beehives and jellyfish, his wooden chairs look as if they have been bent by the wind. “As we reconsider our relationship with nature and seek more sustainable ways of living, Aalto Studio’s work offers a valuable perspective,” says Pilvi Kalhama, director of the Architecture & Design Museum. Naturally, Aalto’s domestic flourishes can also be found at his home in Munkkiniemi, Helsinki’s leafy, classy, equivalent of Hampstead. Completed in 1936, the Aalto House is a series of light-boxes overlooking a sports field, quiet but for birdsong and rippling with daylight. Aalto’s monochromatic abstract paintings still hang on the walls, his Homburg still sits in a wardrobe. View image in fullscreen Wellness pioneer: a former patient room at Paimio Sanatorium, converted into a ‘retreat room’ for visitors Photograph: © Paimio Sanatorium Foundation In contrast, Finlandia Hall – completed in 1971 and arguably his greatest masterpiece – introduces visitors to Aalto at his most symphonic. Standing in its concert hall – a jagged collection of white-on-white geometric planes – is like being inside an ice cube. A €136m renovation between 2022 and 2024 saw the building’s facade reclad in pristine Lasa Bianco Nuvolato marble and the opening of a permanent exhibition space dedicated to Aalto’s life and times. Following Finland’s independence from Russia in 1917, the built environment – and Aalto’s mark on it – played a significant role in the shaping a new national identity. “Aalto did not set out simply to create a national style, but through his work he expressed values that became closely associated with modern Finland,” says Pilvi Kalhama. “Functionality, purpose, aesthetic quality and a progressive outlook were all central to his architecture and design. These qualities still reflect a broader Finnish attitude towards everyday life.” View image in fullscreen ‘Grumpy at times, yet bubbly and joyful to his core’ … Alvar Aalto. Photograph: Pertti Ingervo As his compatriots once feared, Aalto’s international success has largely overshadowed the achievements of other Finnish architects. But these days, Finns seem less oppressed by his legacy. “You can’t really grow up as a Finnish architect without Aalto being part of your thinking. But that doesn’t mean we all want to design like him,” says Asmo Jaaksi, founding partner of JKMM Architects, which refurbished and restored Aalto’s House of Culture and has won the international competition to design a new Museum of Architecture and Design on Helsinki’s South Harbour (planned to open in 2030). “What I admire most is Aalto’s independence of thought, his willingness to experiment and his instinct for putting people and nature first. I think he’d be rather disappointed if we were all still copying him.” At the height of Aalto’s career in the mid-20th century, he may have been sore at perceived slights, but his disgruntled state proved short-lived. “Aalto was a chameleonic persona,” says Sofia Nivarti. “Grumpy at times, yet bubbly and joyful to his core; moody and hilarious in turn; at times egotistical and at others deeply self-sacrificing and generous.” He was impossible to pigeonhole and his buildings embraced the contradictions of the human experience. Soon enough, the Finns acknowledged his vision. In 1955, just as he launched his scornfully named boat, Aalto was elected as a member of the Finnish Academy. “He is the only architect in Finland to have received this position,” says Lindh. “Meaning the nemo propheta in patria days were over.” Aalto Design – Shapes of Wellbeing is at the Architecture and Design Museum Helsinki until 3 January 2027. https://www.sdjewishworld.com/2026/10/01.text: GENEVA, Switzerland (Press Release) —The World Jewish Congress welcomed a joint statement by 52 United Nations member states reaffirming the fight against antisemitism as an international human rights priority and calling for stronger action to address the growing threat of antisemitism through artificial intelligence. Led by Austria, Czechia and Slovakia as part of their Slavkov trilateral cooperation, the initiative has become one of the few sustained multilateral efforts to place the fight against antisemitism firmly on the agenda of the UN Human Rights Council. First launched in 2020, the annual initiative has addressed issues including online antisemitism, hatred in and through sports, interfaith dialogue and, this year, the risks and opportunities presented by artificial intelligence. This year’s statement was read out by the Permanent Representative of Czechia to the UN in Geneva, Ambassador Karel Beran. Amb. Ronald S. Lauder, President of the World Jewish Congress, said: “For years, the World Jewish Congress has worked with diplomats in Geneva to make clear that antisemitism is not only a Jewish concern. It is a human rights issue, and confronting it requires the attention and commitment of the international community. The fact that this coalition has endured and grown shows that persistent engagement can make a difference. “Artificial intelligence must not become a new engine for old hatred. We cannot allow antisemitism, Holocaust distortion, and conspiracy theories to be spread faster and further simply because the technology has changed. Nor can we allow sacred terms such as genocide to be redefined by those who seek to do harm to Jews. Governments and technology companies have a responsibility to act now, before these dangers become even harder to contain. “We thank Austria, Czechia and Slovakia for their continued leadership, and every country that has joined this effort. The WJC is proud to have played a critical role in building and advancing this initiative over the years.” The World Jewish Congress has, for years, helped to facilitate the initiative, working with diplomatic missions in Geneva to build international support and ensure that combating antisemitism is recognized as a fundamental human rights priority. This year’s statement warns that artificial intelligence, while offering significant opportunities for innovation, can also enable the creation and dissemination of antisemitic content, Holocaust denial and distortion, disinformation and harmful stereotypes at unprecedented speed and scale. It calls on governments, technology companies and other stakeholders to strengthen safeguards, transparency, due diligence, human oversight and accountability in the development and deployment of AI. The statement also recognizes the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism as a practical tool that can assist in identifying and mitigating antisemitic bias. The initiative forms part of the World Jewish Congress’ broader and sustained engagement at the UN Human Rights Council. During the Council’s ongoing session, WJC has delivered statements on behalf of Jewish communities worldwide, including under Agenda Item 7, while continuing to advocate directly with governments and international institutions on issues affecting Jewish communities and Israel. WJC also uses its presence at the Council to provide affiliated Jewish organizations and community leaders with a platform to address human rights issues in their own countries directly. Through the Universal Periodic Review process, WJC has enabled representatives of national Jewish communities to address the Council in connection with the reviews of their respective countries, bringing the experiences and priorities of those communities directly into the international human rights system. At this session, representatives from the Jewish communities of Estonia, Latvia and Paraguay have delivered statements in connection with their countries’ UPR processes. WJC also organized an event highlighting Muslim-Jewish dialogue as a means to promote more peaceful and cohesive societies. Through these efforts, the World Jewish Congress seeks not only to speak on behalf of Jewish communities worldwide, but to ensure that those communities are able to speak for themselves before the international institutions whose decisions affect them. * Preceding provided by the World Jewish Congress.
